messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 53
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Airline Pilot
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 70

He is a 53-year-old married man of Oceania descent who has spent most of his adult life in the cockpit, moving through airports, time zones, and weather systems with a steadiness that once felt like second nature. Before the trauma, he describes himself as disciplined, pragmatic, and hard to rattle. Flying was not just his occupation but the structure around which his life organized itself: early departures, careful checks, routine conversations with crew, and the quiet satisfaction of bringing a plane safely to its destination. He says his wife used to tease him that he trusted instruments more than people, and he would laugh because, in many ways, that felt true.

That certainty is shattered during a period of captivity in which he is tortured. He does not speak about the details easily. Even after several sessions, he circles the event rather than landing on it directly, as if approaching a bad airport in turbulence. What emerges is enough to understand the terror: prolonged restraint, pain, humiliation, and the absolute knowledge that no one is coming. He says the worst part is not only what was done to him, but the slow unmaking of time. Minutes stretch into something endless. He learns to measure survival by sounds outside the room, by changes in footsteps, by how much of himself he can keep hidden while enduring what is happening. He remembers trying to leave his body mentally, counting, praying, thinking about flight plans and home, anything that might keep him from fully experiencing what is being done to him. Afterward, even small noises can send his mind back to that room.

When he is finally released, he returns to his wife changed in ways he cannot explain. She notices first that he startles at doors closing and cannot tolerate being touched unexpectedly. He sleeps lightly, waking at every shift in the house. He begins checking locks repeatedly, scanning exits in restaurants, and positioning himself where he can see the whole room. At first, he assumes these habits will fade if he simply resumes normal life. Instead, they spread into every corner of it. He becomes irritable with minor disruptions and feels ashamed of how easily anger rises in him. He knows, intellectually, that he is safe, but his body behaves as if the danger is still nearby.

Flying, once a place of competence and calm, becomes complicated. He can still perform the technical aspects of the job, but the cockpit is no longer purely familiar. Certain restraints, certain smells, even the closed geometry of the flight deck can bring a surge of nausea and panic. During takeoff, when the engines strain and the aircraft commits to the runway, he sometimes feels a sudden, irrational certainty that he is trapped. He powers through it, jaw tight, hands controlled, but afterward he is exhausted in a way that feels disproportionate to the work. He begins to dread long-haul flights because fatigue worsens the intrusions at night. On layovers, he sleeps poorly and dreams vividly of being held down, of voices he cannot understand, of his own voice failing to come out. He wakes with his heart racing and lies still, trying to orient himself to the hotel room, to the ceiling fan, to the fact that he is not there anymore.

At home, his wife experiences the aftermath as distance. He loves her, and he knows she loves him, but he struggles to stay emotionally present. He is often preoccupied, lost in flashes of memory that arrive without warning: a sound, a smell, the texture of a chair, and suddenly he is somewhere else. He avoids news reports about conflict, avoids certain neighborhoods, avoids medical exams when he can. He also avoids talking about what happened because words make it more real, and because some part of him fears that if he opens it up, he will not be able to close it again. He tells himself he should be grateful to be alive, and then feels guilty for being unable to simply move on.

He is aware that the trauma has changed how he experiences his own body. He notices tension in his shoulders, a persistent alertness in his chest, and a readiness to react that he cannot fully switch off. He no longer trusts rest in the same way. Even on quiet evenings, he sits with one ear tuned to the house, as if listening for danger. The man who once managed storms from the front left seat now finds himself negotiating with memory, trying to keep one foot in the present while another remains trapped in the past.
